title: Systems people can live with: operability, simplicity and change
goal: By the end, you can say what makes a system easy to run, turn a promise like "99.9% of payments succeed" into alarms that wake someone only when it matters, tell the complexity a problem needs from the complexity we add, plan changes that can be undone, and weigh renting machines against owning them.
opening:
Picture a smoke alarm in a small flat. It goes off every time someone makes toast. After the fifth false alarm in a week, someone takes the battery out. A month later, a pan catches fire, and nothing beeps.

Nobody in that flat was careless. The alarm screamed at any smoke at all, because that's the easiest rule to build, and the easiest rule is the one everybody builds first. Computer systems get the same alarms, and the people who look after them pull out the same batteries.

The last lesson, Growing past one machine: shared-nothing, shared-disk and the cloud, counted the cost of extra machines in speed. This one counts another cost: the years of looking after a system once it works. In this lesson, we'll build alarms that ring only when it matters, keep a system simple, make its changes easy to undo, and price running it yourself against renting it. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

warmup.q: The payments app promises that 99.9% of payment requests succeed over any 30 days. The team wants to be woken at night only for problems that put that promise in danger. Which of these should wake someone up?
options: 3% of requests failing for 4 minutes
0.35% of requests failing for three days straight
2% of requests failing for an hour, and still going
A total outage that lasts 10 seconds
warmup.why: Count each one against the 0.1% of requests that may fail in 30 days, the month's allowance. 2% failing for an hour spends it 20 times too fast, has already used 2.8% of the month's share, and isn't over: wake someone. The three-day leak spends the most in total (35%), but slowly, at 3.5 times the steady pace, so it can wait for working hours, as long as someone does fix it. The 4-minute blip used 0.28% and the 10-second outage 0.39%, and both were over before anyone could have logged in. The second section turns this counting into alarms.

sections.h: After launch: what makes a system easy to run

try.title: Write a runbook entry
steps: Take this alarm: "the nightly payout job for yesterday hasn't finished by 03:00". The job reads the day's payments, writes each shop's total and sends a payout file to the bank at 04:00.
Write five short lines: what the alarm means, how to confirm it, the safe first action, how to undo that action, and when to call for help.
Check your safe first action: could it make things worse if you're wrong about the cause? If yes, find a smaller one.
try.expect:
One possible entry:

```text
means      the payout file may miss the bank's 04:00 deadline; shops get paid a day late
confirm    the job's status and the last progress line in its log: running, stuck or failed?
first      if failed: rerun it for yesterday's date only (a rerun of one date gives the same totals)
           if running but slow: leave it alone; check the database's processor and locks, estimate the finish
undo       a rerun replaces yesterday's totals; the previous file is kept as payout-<date>.prev
help       at 03:30, if it can't finish by 04:00: wake the payments lead, who can ask the bank for more time
```

The important line is "leave it alone" for a slow job that's still running. Killing and restarting it is the tempting first move, and it throws away all the work the job has done so far.

sections.h: Alarms that ring only when it matters: error budgets and burn rates
sections.body:
The payments app makes a promise: 99.9% of payment requests succeed, over any 30 days. A target like that is an **SLO**, a service level objective, as Latency, percentiles and the tail set it up. The 0.1% it leaves is the **error budget**, the failures you can afford. Over 30 days, that's 43.2 minutes of complete outage, or 0.1% of requests failing all month, or any mix of the two.

The **burn rate** says how fast the budget is going. At a burn rate of 1, it lasts exactly 30 days. If 2% of requests fail, that's 20 times the allowed 0.1%, a burn rate of 20, and the budget is gone in a day and a half.

Most teams first build the smoke alarm from the opening: page someone (send an alert that rings their phone) whenever the last 10 minutes miss 99.9%. It fails both ways. It pages for blips that barely matter: 0.6% of requests failing for 10 minutes uses 0.14% of the month's budget, and still wakes someone up. And a steady leak of 0.35% keeps it ringing for days, until someone silences it. After that, it catches nothing at all.

So alarm on how fast the budget is going, and look at two windows at once. A window is the stretch of time an alarm looks back over, such as the last hour. Here are the three rules that the Google SRE Workbook suggests for a 30-day 99.9% SLO. (It's a book of practice from the team that keeps Google's services running.) A ticket is a note in the team's to-do list, for working hours.

| Action | Long window | Short window | Burn rate | Budget spent when it fires |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| page | 1 hour | 5 minutes | 14.4 | 2% |
| page | 6 hours | 30 minutes | 6 | 5% |
| ticket | 3 days | 6 hours | 1 | 10% |

The long window decides whether enough budget has gone to be worth waking someone. The short window must be over the same line too. It says the problem is still happening, so the alarm stops minutes after the fix instead of an hour later.

The lab replays incidents through these rules, minute by minute. A 2% failure rate for 100 minutes pages at minute 43, with 2.04% of the budget spent, and stops one minute after the fix. The 1-hour window alone would have kept paging until minute 116. A 10-minute total outage fires the fast page in its first minute, the 6-hour page in its third and the ticket in its fifth, and uses 23% of the month. A 0.35% leak for three days never pages. It opens a ticket after about 20 hours, when 10% of the budget is gone, so someone fixes it in working hours.

**A blip that costs nothing shouldn't wake anyone. Page on the budget.**

Alarms are half the job. The other half is an **error budget policy**, agreed before anything goes wrong. For example: "while half the budget is left, release new versions as usual; when it's gone, release only fixes that make the system more reliable, until it recovers". The argument between moving fast and staying up then has an answer before anyone has to win it at 3 a.m.

Alarms tell you that a system is hurting. Next, we'll ask why some systems are so much harder to look after than others.

aside.title: Why not promise 100%?
aside.body: Because nothing delivers it, and chasing it costs more than it's worth. A customer's own phone and network fail more often than a well-run payments app, so they can't tell 99.99% from 100%. Each extra nine costs far more than the last: 99.99% leaves 4.32 minutes a month, barely time to notice a problem, let alone fix it. And a budget of zero means no change is ever safe, so nothing new could ever be released. The budget is what pays for change.

sections.h: Simplicity: keep the complexity the problem needs, and no more
sections.body:
Some systems are easy to change, and others break whenever anyone touches them. The difference is usually complexity: every change has effects that nobody can see in advance. In 1986, Fred Brooks split complexity in two, in an essay called "No Silver Bullet".

**Essential complexity** comes from the problem itself. A card payment first sets money aside, then moves it, and later may be refunded or reversed by the customer's bank. Currencies have different numbers of decimal places: the dollar has two, the Japanese yen none. And networks sometimes deliver the same request twice, so the app must make sure a repeat doesn't charge the card twice. Making a repeat harmless is called idempotency. None of this goes away, however well you build.

**Accidental complexity** comes from how you built it. Three programs each guard against repeats in their own way. Every program that calls another has its own hand-written loop for trying again. A cache, a saved copy of answers, sits in front of a database that was never short of capacity. In a house, the plumbing is essential. Three sets of pipes to the same tap are accidental.

Dan Luu, who writes about software, has argued that the line between the two moves. Much of what looked essential in 1986 was later removed by better tools. So "it's essential" is no reason to stop looking.

The best tool against complexity is a good **abstraction**: an interface that hides a lot of machinery and is shared by many programs. Fix it once, and it's fixed for all of them. SQL, the language most databases understand, is one. You say what you want, and the database decides how to find it on disk. It also keeps programs that run at once from seeing each other's half-finished work, and repairs itself after a crash. A transaction is another: a change to five records happens completely or not at all, and nobody writes the code for "the machine died after record three". Most of this course is about abstractions like these: what each one promises, how it keeps the promise, and what that costs.

The same thinking applies to size. One database on one machine is simpler than a cluster, and five programs are simpler than fifty. The last lesson showed that one machine often wins on speed, too. Choose the simpler design until the load forces the other.

Abstractions leak, though. A query, a question sent to the database, is fast until the database changes its plan, its chosen way of finding the records. A call to another machine looks like a function call until it runs out of time, and you can't tell whether the payment went through. A write says it succeeded, and then the power fails before the data reached the disk. To understand those moments, you need what's under the abstraction: for every data system, the network it talks over and the operating system it runs on.

Leaks are one way a system surprises you. Change is the other, and it's next.

refs.title: Dan Luu: Against essential and accidental complexity

sections.h: Evolvability: make every change easy to undo
sections.body:
A family grows, and the house has to change. Moving the furniture is easy to undo. Knocking down a wall is not, so you check the drawings first. Software changes all the time too: a new way to pay, a new law, ten times the shops, a new team. **Evolvability** is how easily a whole system adapts. It depends on simplicity and on parts that don't lean too hard on each other, and its worst enemy is a change you can't undo.

**A change you can undo in a minute is cheap to try. Make every change one of those.**

Data is what makes changes hard to undo. A program rolls back by deploying, putting into use, its previous version. A migration, a change to how stored data is laid out, often can't. Say it removes a column (one field of a table, like a column in a spreadsheet), or rewrites every row in a new format. Then the old data is gone, and the old program can't read the new. So change data in steps that each keep both directions open, which is called **expand and contract**. Add the new column. Write to both. Fill in the new column for the old rows, a step called a backfill. Switch reads to the new column. Remove the old one only when nothing has read it for a while. The Encoding track builds this properly.

Code changes need the same care. Remember the Google Cloud outage of 12 June 2025, from Faults, failures and the people who run systems? New code with no error handling, and no switch to turn it off, met a setting with blank fields, which a database had copied to every region (every area where Google runs data centres). It crashed in every region at once. A **feature flag** is that switch: it turns a piece of code on or off while the program runs, so undoing it takes seconds instead of a new release. Google's fixes included putting important changes behind flags that start switched off. A staged rollout sends a change, of code or of data, to a few machines first and then to more. One bad change can then break only so much before someone notices.

Some change comes from the law. The GDPR, the European Union's data protection law, gives people the right to have their personal data deleted. That's hard in a log you only append to, and in backups. It's harder still in data already copied into a warehouse for analysis, or used to train a model, a program that learns from old data. The final track of this course returns to it. For now, when you plan where personal data flows, ask how you would delete one person's data everywhere it went.

So far, every choice has assumed that you run the system yourself. Next, we'll weigh that against renting.

try.title: Make a migration reversible
steps: The `merchants` table, one row per shop, has a column `fee_rate`: the share of each payment the company keeps, as a decimal such as 0.029 (2.9%). You want `fee_bp` instead, a whole number of basis points, which are hundredths of a percent (290), and in the end no `fee_rate`. Two programs read the fee: the one that charges it on each payment, and the nightly payout job.
Write the change as a list of deploys and migrations. After each step, write how you would undo it.
Mark the one step that can't be undone, and say what you would check before running it.
try.expect:
One sequence ("nullable" means the column may be left empty; "writers" are the programs that set the fee, and "readers" the ones that use it):

```text
1. add column fee_bp (nullable)                      undo: drop fee_bp
2. deploy: writers set both fee_rate and fee_bp      undo: deploy the previous version
3. backfill fee_bp = round(fee_rate * 10000)         undo: set fee_bp = null
4. deploy: readers use fee_bp (behind a flag)        undo: switch the flag off
5. deploy: writers stop setting fee_rate             undo: deploy step 2's version, rerun step 3 in reverse
6. drop column fee_rate                              cannot be undone
```

Before step 6, check that nothing reads `fee_rate` any more: look at the database's statistics or its log of queries over a full month of payouts, the month's end included. Keep a backup or an archive copy of the column. Steps 1 to 5 can each be undone in minutes, which is why they're cheap to try.

sections.h: Renting or owning: what the cloud's price leaves out
sections.body:
Owning a house and renting a flat both work. Which is cheaper depends on how long you stay and how much your needs change. Every system faces the same question: run the software yourself, or pay someone to run it. The options form a range. At one end, your own code runs on your own machines. In the middle, you run software that others wrote, in your own building or on rented cloud machines. At the other end is a managed service: you reach it only through its API, the list of requests it accepts, and the provider does the running. The usual rule is to run yourself what makes your business different, and buy what everyone needs in the same way.

The cloud wins when the load varies. An analyst's question that needs a hundred machines for two minutes, then nothing for an hour, is cheap to rent and expensive to own. It also wins when you lack the skills: hiring people to run a database well can cost more than the managed service. Owning wins when the load is steady and you already have the people.

The price leaves out what you give up. You can't add a feature the provider lacks. During an outage, you wait. When something is slow, you can't look inside. The provider can raise prices or retire a product, and with no standard API, moving away is expensive. And you trust them with your data, under their country's laws. The running work doesn't vanish, either: someone still plans the spending, learns the provider's limits before hitting them, and wires the services together.

37signals, a small company that makes web apps for teams, is the most-quoted recent case. It paid about $1.5 million a year to keep its files in S3. It bought about $1.5 million of storage hardware from Pure Storage, holding 18 PB (petabytes, millions of gigabytes), and expects it to cost under $200,000 a year to run. It reports saving about $1.3 million a year. In 2025 it moved about 5 PB of unique data, roughly 5 billion files, off S3 in under 10 days without stopping its apps. AWS waived about $250,000 of fees for taking the data out.

These are the company's own numbers, and the $1.3 million compares running costs only. The purchase still has to be paid off, and in five years or so the hardware needs replacing. Spread the purchase over five years, and owning costs about $500,000 a year against $1.5 million. That's still a large saving, for a steady storage load and a team that already runs its own hardware. A company with a spiky load and no such team would get a different answer from the same arithmetic.

Cloud prices shape designs, too. AWS charges for traffic between availability zones, its separate data centres in one region. So Kafka, a program that stores streams of messages, pays for every byte it copies between zones. That bill is why the last lesson's diskless topics exist.

That ends this track, and every number in it rests on something lower down. In the last lesson, Aurora waited for four storage machines in three zones before each change counted, and a serverless function waited through its cold start. When an abstraction leaks, the cause is usually one layer down. It might be a lost piece of network data that has to be sent again, or a slow lookup of a name like example.com. It might be a full waiting line inside the operating system, or a thread paused while another runs. So the next two tracks go down there.

try.title: Run 37signals' numbers for five years
steps: Using the figures in this section, add up five years of S3 against five years of owning: the purchase plus the running costs.
Add something the headline leaves out: say one extra engineer at $200,000 a year to look after the hardware. (That's a guess for the exercise, not a reported figure.) Does owning still win?
Now change the load. Suppose the storage needed doubled in year 3, so a second set of hardware had to be bought in a hurry. What does the cloud give you here that the comparison doesn't price?
try.expect:
```text
S3, 5 years                    5 x $1.5M                      = $7.5M
own, 5 years                   $1.5M + 5 x $0.2M              = $2.5M
own + one extra engineer       $2.5M + 5 x $0.2M              = $3.5M
```

Owning still wins by about $4 million over five years, for this steady load. Doubling in year 3 adds a second purchase of about $1.5 million, plus the wait for delivery and the risk of guessing the size wrong. With S3, the bill grows from year 3, and nobody waits for hardware. That flexibility is what the cloud sells, and it's worth most to the companies whose load is hardest to predict.

compare.title: The same 99.9% SLO, as a naive alarm and as a burn-rate page

b.label: burn rate
b.title: PromQL: page at 14.4x over 1 h AND over 5 min

compare.note: Both are written in PromQL, the query language of Prometheus, a free program that collects metrics. Both work out an error ratio, failed requests divided by all requests, from counters. The left one fires whenever ten minutes fall short of 99.9%, however little budget that costs: in the lab's 2% incident, it fires at once and stays on until 9 minutes after the fix. The right one fires only when the last hour burned the budget 14.4 times too fast, which means 2% of the month's budget is gone, and its 5-minute condition makes it stop as soon as the failures do. A full setup adds the 6-hour and 3-day rules from the table.

worked.title: From an SLO to the minute each alarm fires

steps.say: Start from the SLO. Write the budget down twice: as a share of requests, and as minutes of complete outage.
steps.code:
SLO          99.9% of requests over 30 days
budget       1 - 0.999 = 0.001 of requests
as minutes   0.001 x 30 x 1,440 = 43.2 minutes of full outage

steps.say: Turn each rule's burn rate into a line on the error ratio, the share of requests that fail.
steps.code:
fast burn    14.4 x 0.001 = 1.44% over 1 h and over 5 min
medium burn   6.0 x 0.001 = 0.60% over 6 h and over 30 min
slow burn     1.0 x 0.001 = 0.10% over 3 days and over 6 h

steps.say: When does a 2% incident trip the fast rule? The 1-hour window must reach 1.44%, so 1.44 / 2 of the hour must be bad: 43.2 minutes. The lab counts whole minutes, so it fires at the end of the 44th. The budget spent by then:
steps.code:
burn rate      2% / 0.1% = 20
fires after    ceil(0.72 x 60) = 44 minutes
budget spent   20 x 44 / 43,200 = 2.04%

steps.say: A total outage burns at 1,000, so the hour reaches 1.44% after 0.864 minutes, in the first minute. A 0.35% leak never reaches 0.60% or 1.44%, so it never pages. The 3-day window reaches 0.1% after 0.1 / 0.35 of its 4,320 minutes.
steps.code:
total outage   1.44% of 60 min = 0.864 min        -> page in minute 0
0.35% leak     (0.1 / 0.35) x 4,320 = 1,234.3 min -> ticket after 1,235 minutes,
               10.0% of the budget spent

steps.say: The same arithmetic in Kotlin, as the lab's functions work it out:
steps.code:
fun burnRate(errorRatio: Double, slo: Double) = errorRatio / (1.0 - slo)
fun budgetSpent(burnRate: Double, minutes: Double, windowDays: Int = 30) =
    burnRate * minutes / (windowDays * 1_440.0)

budgetSpent(burnRate(0.02, 0.999), 44.0)       // 0.0204

lab.title: Error budgets and burn-rate alerts, replayed over outages
steps: Run the tests once from the `labs` folder with the command above. Tests are small programs that check your code and say what's wrong. All 8 fail with `NotImplementedError`, Kotlin's way of saying a function's body is still a `TODO`.

Read `Traffic.kt`. It's finished. A history is a list of `Minute`s, each counting all requests and the failed ones. `traffic()` builds a history with incidents in it, and `WORKBOOK_RULES` holds the three rules from the table. Time is virtual: "now" is a position in the list.
In `ErrorBudget.kt`, write `budgetMinutes`, `burnRate` and `budgetSpent`. Each is one line.
Write `errorRatio`: failed requests over all requests, for the window that ends at minute `end`, that minute included. Near the start of the history, use only the minutes that exist.

Write `replay`. For each rule, walk through the minutes. A rule fires when both its windows reach `burnRate × (1 − slo)`. Record an `Alert` when it starts firing, and close it when it stops. Run the tests until all 8 pass: a total outage, a 2% rise in failures, a slow leak, a blip and two separate outages.
hints: A window over minutes `end - n + 1 .. end` starts at `maxOf(0, end - n + 1)`. Being off by one here moves every detection time by a minute, and the tests will say so.

Adding up a 3-day window every minute is 4,320 additions per step. Running totals are faster: keep an array whose entry i holds the failed and total counts of all minutes before minute i. Then each window is two subtractions.

Keep one `firedAt: Int?` per rule while you walk the minutes. Close the alert at the first minute the rule stops firing. If the history ends while a rule is still firing, add its alert with `resolvedAt = null`.
Sort the result with `compareBy({ it.firedAt }, { ruleIndex })`, so alerts that fire in the same minute come out in rule order.

drill.title: Error-budget arithmetic from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking, write three formulas: the error budget of an SLO, in minutes, over a window of some days; the burn rate of an error ratio; and the share of the budget spent by burning at some rate for some minutes. Then use them for a 99.95% SLO over 30 days, with 1% of requests failing for 30 minutes.

answer.src:
budget minutes  = (1 - slo) x days x 1,440
burn rate       = errorRatio / (1 - slo)
budget spent    = burnRate x minutes / (days x 1,440)

99.95% over 30 days:  0.0005 x 30 x 1,440 = 21.6 minutes
1% failing:           burn rate = 0.01 / 0.0005 = 20
30 minutes of it:     20 x 30 / 43,200 = 1.39% of the month's budget

recap: Most of a system's cost comes after it first works. A system is easy to run when it reports what it's doing, depends on no single machine, behaves predictably, has sensible defaults, fixes itself but has a manual override, and has guardrails built into its tools.

An error budget is the share of failures an SLO allows. Page on how fast it burns, over a long and a short window (14.4 over 1 hour and 5 minutes, 6 over 6 hours and 30 minutes), open a ticket at 1 over 3 days, and agree in advance what happens when the budget runs out.

The long window keeps blips from paging; the short window makes the page stop minutes after the fix. A plain 10-minute alarm rings for blips and stays on through slow leaks, until someone silences it.
Essential complexity comes from the problem; accidental complexity comes from how it was built. Good abstractions such as SQL and transactions hide the machinery, but they leak.
Keep changes undoable: expand and contract for data, feature flags and staged rollouts for code. The steps you can't undo are the expensive ones.

The limit: renting or owning depends on how much the load varies and on the skills you have, and headline savings like 37signals' leave out purchase, replacement, staff and flexibility. And every number in this track rests on the network and the operating system, which the next two tracks open up.
closing:
We started with a smoke alarm that rang for every slice of toast until someone took the battery out. Alarms on the error budget ring only when the promise is in danger, and the same care keeps a system simple, its changes undoable and its running costs honest.

Open your phone's notification settings and count the apps that are allowed to interrupt you. For each one, ask the burn-rate question: when it buzzes, does it mean something needs you now? Switch off one that never does.

Next, the Computer networking track fetches one web page with `curl`, a command that downloads a URL, and asks what has to happen before its first byte arrives.

quiz.q: Every card payment calls three other programs, one after another: a fraud check, the card network (the company that passes the payment between banks) and the ledger that keeps the balances. Each one, on its own, meets a 99.9% success SLO. What's the highest success rate you can promise for payments?
options: About 99.7%
About 99.0%
quiz.why: A payment succeeds only if all three calls do: 0.999 × 0.999 × 0.999 ≈ 0.997, about 99.7%, with three times the error budget of any one of them. 99.9% assumes that their failures always happen at the same moments, and they don't. To promise more, you must take one of them off the payment's path (save its answer, fall back to a safe default, or call it later through a queue) or get a tighter SLO from it.

quiz.q: 0.5% of requests start failing, against a 99.9% SLO. What's the burn rate, and how long would the 30-day budget last at that rate?
options: Burn rate 0.5; 60 days
Burn rate 5; 6 days
Burn rate 50; 14 hours
Burn rate 5; 6 hours
quiz.why: Burn rate = 0.5% / 0.1% = 5, so the budget goes five times too fast: 30 days / 5 = 6 days. "Burn rate 0.5" divides the wrong way round. This rate is below 6 and 14.4, so neither page fires. The slow-burn ticket catches it, once the 3-day window has spent 10% of the budget.

quiz.q: Why does each burn-rate rule also need a short window, such as 5 minutes next to the 1-hour window, to be over the line?
options: So that it pages faster when an incident starts
So that it stops firing soon after the problem is fixed, instead of while the long window still remembers the failures
So that short blips trigger a page too
Because Prometheus, the program that collects the numbers, can't work out rates over long windows
quiz.why: The long window decides whether enough budget has gone to matter, and it remembers an incident for up to an hour after it ends. Requiring the short window too means the alarm stops minutes after the fix: in the lab's 2% incident, at minute 101 instead of 116. It doesn't make the page fire sooner. Both windows must agree, so the long one sets the pace.

quiz.q: Which of these is essential complexity in a card-payment app?
options: Handling a request that the network delivered twice, so the card isn't charged twice
Three programs that each guard against repeated requests in their own way
A cache in Redis, a program that keeps data in memory, in front of a database with plenty of spare capacity
A separate small program, with its own database, for each table the app needs
quiz.why: Networks really do deliver some requests twice, so any payment app must make a repeated request harmless: that complexity comes from the problem. The other three come from how the app was built. Three ways of guarding against repeats are two too many. The cache adds the work of keeping it up to date, with no load to justify it. And a program per table splits one set of facts that belong together across network calls.

quiz.q: A team wants to move the nightly payout job from one large server to a cluster service that a cloud provider runs, "so it scales". Using Growing past one machine: shared-nothing, shared-disk and the cloud, what should you measure first?
options: How much faster the cluster gets from 8 to 64 workers
How long one well-written thread takes on the same data, the time any cluster must beat (its COST)
The provider's price per worker per hour
How long the slowest 1 in 100 runs of the job takes
quiz.why: A speed-up curve compares the cluster with itself, and it can look excellent while every size is slower than one thread. COST compares it with one well-written program, and published systems often needed hundreds of cores to win, or never did. Price and scaling matter afterwards, once you know that the cluster beats the simple option at all.

flashcards.front: Why does a burn-rate alarm check a short window as well as a long one?
flashcards.back: The long window says enough budget has gone to matter; the short one says it's still happening, so the alarm stops minutes after the fix.

flashcards.front: Three programs called one after another, each at 99.9%: the best success rate for the whole payment?
flashcards.back: 0.999³ ≈ 99.7%, three times the error budget of any one of them.

flashcards.front: The SRE Workbook's alarm rules for a 30-day 99.9% SLO?
flashcards.back: Page at burn rate 14.4 over 1 h (and 5 min): 2% of the budget. Page at 6 over 6 h (and 30 min): 5%. Ticket at 1 over 3 days (and 6 h): 10%.
Essential comes from the problem (refunds, currencies, repeated requests). Accidental comes from how it was built (three retry loops, a cache nobody needed). The line moves as tools improve.

flashcards.front: How do you change a column's format so each step can be undone?
flashcards.back: Expand and contract: add the new column, write both, fill in the old rows, switch reads, and remove the old column last, once nothing reads it. Only the removal can't be undone.

flashcards.front: What did AWS change after the February 2017 S3 outage?
flashcards.back: The tool that removes servers: it now removes them more slowly, and refuses to take any part below its minimum. A guardrail in the tool, not a warning to the person.
About $1.5M a year for S3; about $1.5M of hardware (18 PB) costing under $200K a year to run; about $1.3M a year saved. Its own numbers, and running costs only.

terms.plain: How easy it is for the people looking after a system to keep it running.
The written procedure for one alarm: what it means, how to check, what to do, how to undo it.
The share of requests an SLO allows to fail, such as 0.1% over 30 days.
An alarm that fires only when the error budget is going too fast, over both a long and a short window.
An agreement, made in advance, about what the team does as the error budget runs low.
Changing stored data in steps that can each be undone: add the new, use both, switch, and remove the old last.
Complexity that comes from the problem itself, and complexity that comes from how the system was built.
A switch that turns a piece of code on or off while the program runs, without a new release.

explain_back.prompt: Your manager asks why you want to delete the alarm "failures above 1% for 5 minutes" and replace it with burn-rate alarms. Explain it in your own words, with numbers.
explain_back.answer: Our SLO is 99.9% of requests succeeding over 30 days, so the error budget is 0.1% of requests, about 43 minutes of complete outage a month. The current alarm ignores that. It wakes someone for a 5-minute blip that uses a tiny part of the budget, and it never fires for a 0.5% leak that would empty the whole budget in six days. A burn-rate alarm pages when we're spending the budget too fast for long enough to matter: 14.4 times too fast over an hour means 2% of the month is already gone, and 6 times over six hours means 5%. Each rule also checks a short window, so the page stops minutes after the fix. A slow burn over three days opens a ticket instead of waking anyone. We get fewer pages, and each one means real budget is going.

deeper.body:
**Your SLO can't beat the programs it depends on.** If a payment calls the fraud check, the card network and the ledger one after another, and each fails on its own 0.1% of the time, the payment fails about 0.3% of the time: 0.999³ ≈ 99.7%. Calling them at the same time doesn't help, unless any one answer is enough, which is what hedged requests (Latency, percentiles and the tail) and spare copies buy. So an SLO also guides design. It tells you which programs must come off the payment's path, through a saved answer, a safe default, or a call made later through a queue.

**Quiet services.** Burn-rate alarms need enough requests for a ratio to mean something. At 10 requests an hour, a 99.9% budget over 30 days is about 7 failed requests, so one failure spends 13.9% of the month. The Workbook suggests sending made-up test requests, putting several small services under one SLO, or accepting a lower SLO for them.

**Promises about speed.** The same machinery works for speed. Count a request as bad if it took longer than, say, 300 ms, and the error ratio becomes the share of slow requests. That turns the percentiles of Latency, percentiles and the tail into a budget: "99% of payments answered in under 300 ms" allows 1% of requests to be slow, and a burn-rate alarm tells you when they're becoming slow too fast.

**Google's other fix.** After the June 2025 outage, Google also committed to sending out data that's copied to every region in stages, with time to check each stage, the same staged rollout it already used for code.

**Where the words come from.** SRE stands for site reliability engineering, Google's name for the job of keeping its services running. The 1-hour and 6-hour pages and the 3-day ticket come from chapter 5 of its Workbook, which also explains why simpler rules (one window, or a fixed error rate) page too often or too late.
